name: Central Sikhote-Alin
blurb: Korean pine, wapiti and boar feed the Amur tiger in the Far East forest.

tip.title: Remove the Korean pine
tip.text: Pine seeds feed boar, bears, sables and nutcrackers. Set Korean pine to -100% and watch those seed eaters, then the tiger that preys on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Summer light drives growth in the forest canopy and understorey of the mountain slopes.

nodes.name: Summer monsoon rain
nodes.desc: The Russian Far East gets its rain mostly in the warm season, feeding the lush mixed forest on the coastal slopes.

nodes.name: Forest soil & nutrients
nodes.desc: Leaf litter and decaying wood build the soil that the trees and shrubs draw on.

nodes.name: Fungi, bacteria & insects
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, wood and carcasses, returning nutrients to the forest soil.

nodes.name: Korean pine
nodes.desc: Its seeds stay in the cones until birds such as the nutcracker carry them off. The mixed Korean pine and broadleaf forest is described as the tiger's home forest.

nodes.name: Mongolian oak
nodes.desc: A common broadleaf tree of the region whose acorns are a food for boar, deer and bears.

nodes.name: Maples & other broadleaf trees
nodes.desc: Maples, limes and other broadleaf trees mixed into the forest, offering leaves, twigs and bark to browsers.

nodes.name: Honeysuckle & berry shrubs
nodes.desc: Honeysuckle is one of several berry-bearing shrubs and vines that Ussuri brown bears eat in the region.

nodes.name: Tree lichens
nodes.desc: Lichens growing on trunks and branches. They are the near-total winter food of musk deer.

nodes.name: Spotted nutcracker
nodes.desc: Collects Korean pine seeds in autumn and caches them, which is how the pine gets dispersed.

nodes.name: Siberian chipmunk
nodes.desc: A small seed-eating ground rodent of the forest, and a prey item for foxes, sables and bears in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Gray red-backed vole
nodes.desc: A small rodent of the forest floor that feeds many predators; GloBI records it as eaten by bears and foxes.

nodes.name: Siberian musk deer
nodes.desc: A small, nocturnal, fanged but herbivorous deer that lives on rocky forested slopes; lichens make up about 99% of its winter diet.

nodes.name: Sika deer
nodes.desc: A medium deer of the Primorye forests and one of the main prey of tigers in scat studies.

nodes.name: Manchurian wapiti
nodes.desc: Adapted to mixed deciduous forest. Tiger distribution has been found to follow wapiti distribution closely.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: An omnivore that digs for roots and eats acorns and nuts. In the Amur region, boar and wapiti make up about 80% of tiger prey.

nodes.name: Sable
nodes.desc: A forest marten; the reserve was founded in 1935 to protect its population.

nodes.name: Red fox
nodes.desc: A small generalist hunter that GloBI records eating rodents, chipmunks, birds and hares.

nodes.name: Ussuri brown bear
nodes.desc: Mostly vegetarian, eating acorns, Korean pine seeds and berries. Bears steal about 35% of tiger kills in Sikhote-Alin and can also kill tigers.

nodes.name: Amur tiger
nodes.desc: Preys mainly on wapiti, wild boar, sika and roe deer. Tigers also suppress wolves, which are scarce in tiger forests.
